content.intro: Learn understanding virtual environments through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding Virtual Environments matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines understanding virtual environments as part of development environment and project setup. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: Purpose of virtual environments; Creating and activating a virtual environment; Deactivating an environment; Isolating project dependencies; Managing environments across operating systems. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: Purpose of virtual environments
items.text: A virtual environment isolates Python packages for this project. Activate it before installing packages or running commands, and make sure the editor and terminal use the same interpreter.

items.title: Creating and activating a virtual environment
items.text: Create the environment with `python -m venv .venv`, then activate it using the command for your shell. Do not commit the environment folder; recreate it from documented dependencies.

items.title: Deactivating an environment
items.text: Deactivation changes the current shell back to its previous interpreter context; it does not uninstall packages from the environment.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Understanding Virtual Environments
content_blocks.code:
python -m venv .venv
# Windows PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip --version
python -m django --version
content_blocks.expected_output: The commands run package/version checks inside the activated environment.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Open a local project using the documented Django 6.1-compatible Python environment. If this snippet depends on model names, URL configuration, settings, or an optional package, add those prerequisites before running it. Otherwise inspect it as a static example. CodeLeaf browser preview does not execute Django/Python server code.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to Purpose of virtual environments. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to describe understanding virtual environments, explain the listed topics, inspect the example, and choose an appropriate verification step. Keep the scope and version caveat visible when sharing your solution.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a framework fragment without its imports, configuration, model, or URL context.
common_mistakes.why: The snippet may be incomplete when separated from a Django project.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the stated prerequisites and run the relevant management check or focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting input or relying only on a happy-path example.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid values, unauthorized requests, or concurrent activity can violate assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and add a negative or boundary test.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating the development sample as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Production hosting, secrets, storage, monitoring and resource limits differ from local use.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the current deployment/security references and document untested areas.
